Bridge node E scores 1.00 after normalizing, the tail node F 0.76 and the hub C only 0.34, while A and G score 0." width="100%"} Bridging centrality (Hwang et al., 2008) identifies nodes that act as bridges between densely connected communities. It combines the *bridging coefficient* (a local measure of how much a node links to otherwise-separated groups) with *betweenness centrality* (global importance for shortest paths): $$\mathrm{BrC}(v) = \mathrm{BC}_{\mathrm{coeff}}(v) \times \mathrm{betweenness}(v)$$ where the bridging coefficient is: $$\mathrm{BC}_{\mathrm{coeff}}(v) = \frac{1/d(v)}{\sum_{j \in N(v)} 1/d(j)}$$ The bridging coefficient is large when a node has few neighbors but those neighbors have many, which is the typical position of a node sitting *between* two dense regions rather than inside one. Betweenness alone often ranks the busy nodes at the edge of a cluster almost as highly as the true connector; multiplying by the coefficient separates them. This makes bridging centrality useful for: - finding the connectors between modules in protein interaction or gene networks - spotting brokers between communities in social and organizational networks - identifying fragile links between regions in infrastructure networks The betweenness term is the same normalized betweenness computed by `betweenness_centrality()`, so the cost is dominated by an all-pairs shortest-path computation. Edge weights are ignored. In directed graphs, degrees and neighbors refer to outgoing edges. Isolated nodes score `0`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [normalized]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), divide every score by the largest one so the top node scores exactly `1.0`; this makes the ranking easy to read but loses the absolute scale. If `False`, return the raw product of the bridging coefficient and normalized betweenness, which can be compared across graphs. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Column name used to store the scores in the node DataFrame. If `None` (default), the column is named `"bridging_centrality"`. An existing column with the same name is overwritten. Only used when `return_dict=` is `False`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the scores as a dictionary and leave the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), store the scores under `attr_name=` and return the graph for method chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to bridging centrality scores. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two four-node cliques (A to D and E to H) are joined through a single connector X. Plain betweenness ranks the clique members D and E almost as highly as X, since every path between the cliques passes through all three: ::: {#17982b56 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G", "H", "X"]) for clique in (["A", "B", "C", "D"], ["E", "F", "G", "H"]): for i, u in enumerate(clique): for v in clique[i + 1:]: graph.add_edge(u, v) graph.add_edge("D", "X").add_edge("X", "E") between = graph.betweenness_centrality(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): round(s, 3) for nid, s in sorted(between.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.0, 'C': 0.0, 'D': 0.536, 'E': 0.536, 'F': 0.0, 'G': 0.0, 'H': 0.0, 'X': 0.571} ``` ::: ::: Bridging centrality separates them clearly. X has only two neighbors, each with high degree, so its bridging coefficient is large, while D and E sit inside dense cliques. After normalization X scores `1.0` and D and E fall to about `0.16`: ::: {#8047368b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} bridging = graph.bridging_centrality(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): round(s, 3) for nid, s in sorted(bridging.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.0, 'C': 0.0, 'D': 0.156, 'E': 0.156, 'F': 0.0, 'G': 0.0, 'H': 0.0, 'X': 1.0} ``` ::: ::: With `normalized=False` the raw scores are returned instead, so the top value is no longer pinned to `1.0`: ::: {#ee417a23 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} raw = graph.bridging_centrality(normalized=False, return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): round(s, 3) for nid, s in sorted(raw.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.0, 'C': 0.0, 'D': 0.089, 'E': 0.089, 'F': 0.0, 'G': 0.0, 'H': 0.0, 'X': 0.571} ``` ::: :::
